prompt.context: Your client is an industrial manufacturer of cranes. They are a French company and have recently acquired a U.S. business in order to expand their product offering and enter the U.S. market. The two products they have after the acquisition are mobile cranes and tower cranes. The combined company holds approximately 60% of the market. Currently, the tower business, used for skyscrapers, is located in Europe, and the mobile business, used for building highways, is located in the U.S. Prior to the acquisition, the company did have a small mobile manufacturer in Europe that they still retain.
prompt.question: The company has brought you and your team in to determine how to reduce redundancy and maintain a single face to the customer. The client also wants to explore the possibility of expanding mobile cranes into Europe and tower cranes into the U.S. Should they build new facilities or ship products?

clarifying_info.q: How are products currently distributed to customers?
clarifying_info.a: 60% of revenues come from leases through a dealer (manufacturer -> dealer -> construction firm); 40% come from direct leases (manufacturer -> construction firm).
When dealers are involved in leasing equipment, they are responsible for equipment repairs. They must also know the product well.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current market share breakdown by product and region?
clarifying_info.a: Tower cranes: Europe 80%, U.S. 20%. Mobile cranes: Europe 40%, U.S. 70%. Combined global share is approximately 60%.

clarifying_info.q: Have dealers been informed of the acquisition?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. The information was communicated to dealers, who now have an expectation of lower costs resulting from redundancy elimination.

clarifying_info.q: What is the impact on dealers from the expanded product catalog?
clarifying_info.a: Dealers will now have larger costs since they must learn the sales pitch for the new catalog of products and be prepared to service them. They will need higher profit margins to offset these costs.

framework: Understand current distribution channels: dealer-based (60%) vs. direct (40%), and implications for the acquisition integration
Analyze the impact on dealer relationships: expanded catalog increases dealer costs; managing these relationships is key to retaining market share
Evaluate mobile crane expansion into Europe: three options — expand existing European facility, build/navigate new European sites, or ship from U.S.
Evaluate tower crane expansion into the U.S.: two options — build a new U.S. facility or ship from Europe
Compare options on tariffs, capital investment, lead time, competition, and demand certainty
Provide a recommendation with risks and next steps

questions.prompt: What are the options and trade-offs for expanding mobile cranes into Europe?
questions.guidance: Strong answer covers three options: (1) Expand the existing small European mobile facility — low risk, but capacity must be assessed; no action until it reaches 100% capacity. (2) Build/navigate new European sites — advantage: no tariffs; disadvantages: finding a suitable location and significant capital investment. (3) Ship from the U.S. — advantage: can use excess inventory; disadvantages: tariffs, competitive pressure, and long lead times.

questions.prompt: What are the options and trade-offs for expanding tower cranes into the U.S.?
questions.guidance: Strong answer covers two options: (1) Build a new U.S. facility — advantage: no tariffs; disadvantage: customer demand in the U.S. has not been proven and a way to measure demand must be found before committing capital. (2) Ship from Europe — disadvantages: tariffs, competition from existing U.S. crane manufacturers, and long lead times.

questions.prompt: How should the client manage the dealer relationship given the expanded product catalog?
questions.guidance: Dealers face higher costs (training on new products, servicing new SKUs). Client should proactively initiate dealer training programs and consider increasing dealer profit margins to offset these costs. Managing dealer relationships is critical because 60% of revenue flows through the dealer channel, and dealers already expect cost savings from the acquisition.

brainstorming.prompt: What risks and considerations should the client keep in mind as it moves forward with expansion?

categories.name: Demand risk
ideas: Demand for cranes is cyclical and tied to construction activity; it might decrease over time, making capital expenditure redundant
Tower crane demand in the U.S. has not been proven — need to find a way to measure it before building a facility

categories.name: Product risk
ideas: A hybrid product (between mobile and tower, for small-to-mid-size projects) may not be accepted well by buyers
Expanded catalog increases complexity for dealers and service teams

categories.name: Dealer relationship risk
ideas: Dealers expected lower costs post-acquisition; failing to manage this expectation could damage relationships
Higher costs for dealers (training, servicing new products) require higher margins, compressing client economics

categories.name: Operational / supply chain risk
ideas: Shipping cross-Atlantic incurs tariffs and long lead times, reducing competitiveness
Capacity constraints at the existing European mobile facility limit near-term expansion volume

categories.name: Competitive risk
ideas: Competitors in both regions may respond aggressively to market entry
Local manufacturers in each region have incumbent advantages on service and lead time

categories.name: Geographic expansion
ideas: Opportunity to expand beyond Europe and the U.S. to other continents once integration is stable

recommendation: For mobile expansion into Europe: first fully utilize and expand the existing small European mobile facility before committing to a new greenfield site or cross-Atlantic shipping; this minimizes capital outlay and avoids tariffs

For tower expansion into the U.S.: rather than an entirely new facility, consider converting an existing U.S. facility to produce a hybrid product (between mobile and tower) capable of handling small-to-mid-size projects — this requires less capital than a new build and can capture unmet demand while limiting downside risk
Proactively manage dealer relationships by initiating product training programs and reviewing dealer margin structures to ensure they can profitably represent the expanded catalog
risks: Demand may decline due to construction cycle downturns, stranding capital investment
The hybrid product concept may face buyer resistance if it is not perceived as a direct substitute for either crane type
Dealers who do not receive adequate margin relief may de-prioritize the client's products in favor of competitors
next_steps: Assess current capacity utilization of the existing European mobile facility to determine timeline for expansion
Conduct U.S. market research to quantify demand for tower/hybrid cranes before committing to facility conversion capital
Engage dealer network with a formal communication plan, training rollout, and revised margin structure
Explore expansion opportunities in other continents once European and U.S. integration is complete
